The building complex incorporates the design traditions of [Indo-Islamic](/wiki/Indo-Islamic_architecture "Indo-Islamic architecture") and [Mughal architecture](/wiki/Mughal_architecture "Mughal architecture"). It employs symmetrical constructions with the usage of various shapes and symbols. While the mausoleum is constructed of white [marble](/wiki/Marble "Marble") inlaid with [semi-precious stones](/wiki/Semi-precious_stones "Semi-precious stones"), [red sandstone](/wiki/Red_sandstone "Red sandstone") was used for other buildings in the complex similar to the Mughal era buildings of the time. The construction project employed more than 20,000 workers and artisans under the guidance of a board of architects led by [Ustad Ahmad Lahori](/wiki/Ustad_Ahmad_Lahori "Ustad Ahmad Lahori"), the emperor's court architect. The complex was designed and executed by a multinational board of artisans and supervisors, including [Ottoman](/wiki/Ottoman_Empire "Ottoman Empire") dome designer Ismail Afandi; Persian architects [Ustad Isa](/wiki/Ustad_Isa "Ustad Isa"), [Isa Muhammad Effendi](/wiki/Isa_Muhammad_Effendi "Isa Muhammad Effendi"), and Puru; chief calligrapher Amanat Khan Shirazi; finial caster Qazim Khan; and masonry supervisors Muhammad Hanif, Mir Abdul Karim, and Mukkarimat.[[5]](#cite_note-5)

The Taj Mahal was designated as a [UNESCO World Heritage Site](/wiki/UNESCO_World_Heritage_Site "UNESCO World Heritage Site") in 1983 for being "the jewel of [Islamic art](/wiki/Islamic_art "Islamic art") in India and one of the universally admired masterpieces of the world's heritage". It is regarded as one of the best examples of Mughal architecture and a symbol of Indian history. The Taj Mahal is a major tourist attraction and attracts more than five million visitors a year. In 2007, it was declared a winner of the [New 7 Wonders of the World](/wiki/New_7_Wonders_of_the_World "New 7 Wonders of the World") initiative. [Euro 1980](/wiki/UEFA_Euro_1980 "UEFA Euro 1980") was the last tournament for which the Total Football team qualified. Despite the tournament format being expanded that year they did not advance past the group stage as they finished behind Czechoslovakia by goal difference.[[27]](#cite_note-28)

Veterans such as Krol and Rensenbrink retired soon afterwards and the Netherlands hit a low point in their history: they missed the [1982 World Cup](/wiki/1982_FIFA_World_Cup "1982 FIFA World Cup") in Spain, [Euro 1984](/wiki/UEFA_Euro_1984 "UEFA Euro 1984") in France, and the [1986 World Cup](/wiki/1986_FIFA_World_Cup "1986 FIFA World Cup") in Mexico; they missed the French tournament by virtue of goals scored when [Spain](/wiki/Spain_national_football_team "Spain national football team") scored twelve in the final game against [Malta](/wiki/Malta_national_football_team "Malta national football team"). While both teams had the same [goal difference](/wiki/Goal_difference "Goal difference") (+16), Spain qualified having scored two more goals than the Netherlands.[[28]](#cite_note-29) During the qualification stage for the 1986 World Cup the Netherlands finished in second place and advanced to the play-offs against neighbours Belgium. After losing the first leg 1–0 in [Brussels](/wiki/Brussels "Brussels"), they held a 2–0 lead at [Rotterdam](/wiki/Rotterdam "Rotterdam") with a few minutes remaining. [Georges Grün](/wiki/Georges_Gr%C3%BCn "Georges Grün")'s header in the 84th minute resulted in the Netherlands' elimination as Belgium advanced to the World Cup on [away goals](/wiki/Away_goals_rule "Away goals rule").[[29]](#cite_note-1986WCQ-30)[[30]](#cite_note-31)

Nippon Professional Baseball consists of two leagues, the [Central League](/wiki/Central_League "Central League") and the [Pacific League](/wiki/Pacific_League "Pacific League"), which each have six teams. There are also two secondary-level professional minor leagues, the [Eastern League](/wiki/Eastern_League_(Japanese_baseball) "Eastern League (Japanese baseball)") and the [Western League](/wiki/Western_League_(Japanese_baseball) "Western League (Japanese baseball)"), that play shorter schedules for developing players in the so called "Farm System". NPB teams are allowed to have more than one minor league team as long those others are outside of the established farm/minor league system, with the [Fukuoka SoftBank Hawks](/wiki/Fukuoka_SoftBank_Hawks "Fukuoka SoftBank Hawks") and [Yomiuri Giants](/wiki/Yomiuri_Giants "Yomiuri Giants") being the only teams taking advantage of this. As of 2023, the Hawks have three minor league teams,[[4]](#cite_note-4) the Giants have two, and the other ten teams only have one minor league team each. Teams below the Eastern and Western Leagues play exhibition matches against various teams of collegiate, [industrial](/wiki/Baseball_in_Japan#Amateur_baseball "Baseball in Japan"), [Shikoku Island League Plus](/wiki/Shikoku_Island_League_Plus "Shikoku Island League Plus"), and other NPB minor league statuses.

The Central League and Pacific League operate as separate entities, unlike the [four major professional sports leagues of North America](/wiki/Major_professional_sports_leagues_in_the_United_States_and_Canada "Major professional sports leagues in the United States and Canada") and the [KBO League](/wiki/KBO_League "KBO League") in [South Korea](/wiki/South_Korea "South Korea"), whose leagues each operate as one singular entity. Nesbitt was born to John and [Kathleen Nesbitt](/wiki/Kathleen_Nesbitt "Kathleen Nesbitt"), both music teachers in County Tipperary, Ireland. She has a sister, Frances, and four brothers, Seán, Michael, Noel and Karl, all of whom are musicians. She has been a piano player since the age of four, and began playing the violin at age six.

Her formal musical studies began at The Ursuline Convent in [Thurles](/wiki/Thurles "Thurles"), [County Tipperary](/wiki/County_Tipperary "County Tipperary") and progressed through the [Waterford Institute of Technology](/wiki/Waterford_Institute_of_Technology "Waterford Institute of Technology") and the [Cork School of Music](/wiki/Cork_School_of_Music "Cork School of Music"), during which time she participated in the [National Youth Orchestra of Ireland](/wiki/National_Youth_Orchestra_of_Ireland "National Youth Orchestra of Ireland"). Nesbitt completed postgraduate studies at [Royal Academy of Music](/wiki/Royal_Academy_of_Music "Royal Academy of Music") and [Trinity College of Music](/wiki/Trinity_College_of_Music "Trinity College of Music") in London under [Emanuel Hurwitz](/wiki/Emanuel_Hurwitz "Emanuel Hurwitz").[[3]](#cite_note-3)

Besides her family, Nesbitt has stated that her influences range from [Itzhak Perlman](/wiki/Itzhak_Perlman "Itzhak Perlman") and [Michael Coleman](/wiki/Michael_Coleman_(Irish_musician) "Michael Coleman (Irish musician)") to bluegrass artist [Alison Krauss](/wiki/Alison_Krauss "Alison Krauss") and rock's [David Bowie](/wiki/David_Bowie "David Bowie") and [Sting](/wiki/Sting_(musician) "Sting (musician)").[[4]](#cite_note-4)

Nesbitt has been married to Jim Mustapha Jr., Celtic Woman's then-lighting director, since 2011.[[5]](#cite_note-5)

It won for Best Picture, Best Actress, Best Supporting Actress, Best Director, Best Screenplay, Best Cinematography, Best Art Direction, and Best Editing, and received two further honorary awards for its use of equipment and color (it also became the first color film to win Best Picture).[[60]](#cite_note-Oscars1940-65)[[61]](#cite_note-Randall-66)
